Dwight caught it. Filed it away without comment. Now was not the time. He looked back at Danny instead — at the cut on his temple and the set of his jaw and the particular vacancy behind his eyes that Dwight recognised from the inside — and felt the last piece slide into place with the specific, terrible quality of something that had been true for a while before he'd been ready to see it. Six. There had always been six. Danny hadn't wandered into their trial by accident; he had been there when Dwight and David entered the building. He was the sixth, the numbers settled and even like every ritual trial that came before, and the Entity had known that when She set the whole thing in motion. Which meant the count had been right all along. Which meant nobody was marked. Which meant all of them were. Dwight kept his face still and his mouth shut and looked at the waterline climbing the wall behind Danny, and did not say any of this out loud. They pushed again. Slammed. Wedged. Cursed. Nothing. The roar was constant; water hammering from ceilings, gushing from ruptured lockers, sluicing down halls, but within the shift was happening quietly — beneath the roar of water and the crash of falling debris, something subtler was bleeding through. Fatigue. Disbelief. The door work continued — Jake and David and Leon cycling through angles, trying leverage points the wood had already refused, finding new sections of frame to test and receiving the same answer from all of them. The sounds of it were the same sounds they'd been making for the better part of an hour. Impact. Resistance. Reset. Impact again. But something had gone out of it. Not the effort, exactly. The belief behind the effort. The quality of each strike shifted by degrees, the force behind it becoming less about breaking through and more about having something to do with hands that didn't know what else to try. The pauses between attempts got longer. The resets got slower. Nobody called it. Nobody said the word. They just gradually stopped pretending the door was going to open and kept working it anyway because stopping meant standing in chest-high water with nowhere to look that wasn't bad. David was the last to still. He'd been running on something past exhaustion for a while now — some reserve below the reserve, stubbornness metabolised into fuel — and it had finally spent itself against a door that hadn't moved a millimetre in response to any of it. His shoulder sagged against the door, and he wiped the water from his face with the back of his wrist. His eyes darted around the hallway around them, the dark water and the debris and the five — six — people standing in it, as if the answer might be somewhere in the room if he just kept his eyes moving long enough to find it. Leon's hand moved over the doorframe one more time, slow and deliberate, fingers reading the grain like there was something in the wood he hadn't found yet. His eyes tracked the foyer in quick passes — ceiling, walls, the hallway, back to the door — as if the trick to opening it had just been missed somehow. His jaw was tight, eyes unfocused, every inch of his mind trying to slap down the question of just how much time they had. Jake had backed into the corner where the foyer met the hall, shoulders against the junction of two walls, arms wrapped around himself. His hands moved over his own forearms in short restless passes. His eyes were down, following the shadows against the walls as if tracking the waterline creeping higher. Danny had listed sideways until his shoulder found Orela's, the effort of staying upright more exhausting than it was worth in the moment. She'd let him, which said something about the state of things. He was looking at the group with an expression that had shed all of its earlier distance — watching the survivors like he was one of them now — and realizing just how little that meant down here. One hand twitched idly at his side, reaching for the phantom of a knife that was long lost. Orela kept her eyes on the door. Nobody had to say it. They could all feel it pressing in around them. The basement had filled from the ground up, patient and complete, until it had nowhere left to go but through the ceiling. The main doors had taken everything they had and given nothing back. The back door had done the same. The windows Jake had worked on in what felt like another lifetime had absorbed the crowbar without comment. The walls bled water from every seam and showed no sign of running dry. The geometry of the building had doubled and tripled and rearranged itself they could barely recognize the layout anymore. They had tried everything the building had presented them with. The building had not run out of answers. They stood in the roar of it — six people in chest-high water in a foyer that was still shrinking — the stillness between them fragile and uneasy. Silence pulsed under the roar of the water. "...Did you try the side entrance yet?" The words came out thin and ragged, half swallowed by the noise, Danny pushing himself upright from Orela's shoulder with a wince as his ribs filed a formal complaint. Heads turned. Leon’s eyes narrowed, his breath harsh as he gave a single tired laugh, incredulous. "The Entity always puts a wall there. Hardly ever a door. And on the off chance it IS..."
